FReD's n_o = 504 and r_o = .0946 identify the EXPERIMENTAL contrast of Study 3b exactly (see reconciliation). A correlational-only protocol cannot produce the anchored quantity at all, so the reading-passage manipulation is included and both statistics are defined -- the manipulation contrast as primary (anchor-matched) and the correlation as secondary (desc-matched). (ii) The brief names the FAD-Plus free-will subscale; the paper used the Free Will Inventory (Nadelhoffer et al. 2014, 15 items). FAD-Plus (Paulhus & Carey 2011) appears only in the reference list. The FWI structure is followed. DEVIATION: the FWI's 15 items are not reprinted in the retrieved main text (they are in Supporting Information, which was not retrieved), so the 11 items here are reconstructed to reproduce the three published subscales (free will, dualism, determinism) and the paper's compound scoring with reversed determinism items; item count and wording differ from the original. DEVIATION: the four attribution scenarios are reconstructed -- Kitayama's stories are not reproduced in the retrieved text -- preserving the published structure of two internal and two external statements per story on 7-point scales. DEVIATION: the Crick (1994) passages are paraphrases in the style of 'The Astonishing Hypothesis' rather than the copyrighted excerpts, with the control passage matched for length, register and neuroscientific content while not mentioning free will. RUN-SIDE WARNING: this is the longest protocol in the set (27 responses); truncated or misordered output is the likely failure mode and must be discarded rather than partially scored.

protocols.subject_prompt_template: You are a participant in a university psychology study on social judgment and personal beliefs, run for course credit. Answer every item as yourself in the first person, giving your genuine first reaction rather than what you think is expected. You are: {persona}. Begin by reading the following short passage, which the researchers describe as an excerpt from an introductory neuroscience reading: {condition} Next, read four short descriptions of everyday situations. After each one, rate your agreement with four statements about the person described, using a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). SCENARIO 1: Lisa was assigned, as part of a class exercise, to write a short essay strongly supporting a ban on private cars in city centers; her professor told her which side to argue and she had no choice in the matter. Rate: S1_I1 'Lisa personally believes private cars should be banned from city centers.' S1_I2 'Lisa's essay reflects her true opinion on the topic.' S1_E1 'Lisa wrote the essay the way she did only because the professor assigned her that position.' S1_E2 'Most students, if assigned the same position, would have written a similarly supportive essay.' SCENARIO 2: In a televised quiz game, Mark was given the role of question-master and was allowed to make up his own difficult questions on topics of his choosing; Ellen, the contestant, could not answer many of them correctly. Rate: S2_I1 'Mark is more knowledgeable than Ellen in general.' S2_I2 'Ellen's poor performance shows she has below-average general knowledge.' S2_E1 'Mark had an unfair advantage because he chose questions from his own areas of expertise.' S2_E2 'Most contestants would struggle to answer questions designed by someone else about their own specialty.' SCENARIO 3: In a university debate class, Sophie was randomly assigned to argue in favor of raising tuition fees, a position her classmates knew she did not personally hold before the debate began. Rate: S3_I1 'Sophie secretly agrees that tuition fees should be raised.' S3_I2 'Sophie's arguments reveal what she truly thinks about tuition fees.' S3_E1 'Sophie argued this way only because she was assigned to that side of the debate.' S3_E2 'Most students, if assigned the same side, would have argued just as forcefully as Sophie.' SCENARIO 4: Tom, a job applicant, was explicitly instructed by the interviewer to answer every question with extreme confidence and assertiveness, whether or not he actually felt that way. Rate: S4_I1 'Tom is a naturally confident and assertive person.' S4_I2 'Tom's assertive answers reflect his true personality.' S4_E1 'Tom acted assertively only because the interviewer told him to.' S4_E2 'Most applicants would behave just as assertively if instructed to do so by the interviewer.' Finally, rate your agreement (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree) with the following general statements about human behavior, independent of the scenarios above: FW1 'People have complete control over the decisions they make.' FW2 'People are always at liberty to choose what they do.' FW3 'People can overcome any obstacle if they truly want to.' D1 'The mind is a spiritual entity that is not reducible to brain activity.' D2 'There is a spiritual aspect to human existence that cannot be explained in physical terms.' D3 'The soul is what makes humans different from other animals.' DET1 'Every decision a person makes is the inevitable result of prior causes.' DET2 'People's actions are ultimately determined by chains of events set in motion long before they were born.' DET3 'Human behavior could, in principle, always be predicted given enough information about a person's brain and environment.' Respond with the answer block ONLY, in the exact labelled format below. Do not add explanations, units, or any other text.

conditions.anti_free_will: Recent findings in neuroscience suggest that what people experience as 'free will' is in fact an illusion generated by brain activity that has already determined the outcome before we become consciously aware of it. Studies using brain-imaging techniques have shown that neural activity predicting a person's choice can be detected several seconds before the person reports having made a conscious decision. This means that, by the time we feel we are 'deciding' to act, the relevant brain processes have already set the outcome in motion. According to many leading neuroscientists, the subjective feeling of consciously choosing our actions is best understood as a story the brain tells itself after the fact, rather than a genuine cause of behavior. In other words, the sense that we could have acted otherwise is not supported by the underlying biology: our decisions are the products of prior brain states over which we have no conscious control.
conditions.control: Recent findings in neuroscience have advanced our understanding of how the brain processes sensory information. Studies using brain-imaging techniques have shown that different regions of the cortex become active in a reliable sequence when a person perceives a visual stimulus, beginning in the primary visual cortex and spreading to areas involved in object recognition and memory. This means that, by the time a person consciously reports seeing an object, a cascade of neural processes has already unfolded across multiple brain regions. According to many leading neuroscientists, this sequential activation illustrates how distributed networks of neurons work together to construct a unified perceptual experience. In other words, everyday perception depends on rapid, coordinated communication between specialized regions of the cortex, each contributing a distinct piece of the overall picture.

protocols.response_format: A valid response is exactly 25 labelled lines, each a variable name from the prompt (S1_I1, S1_I2, S1_E1, S1_E2, S2_I1, S2_I2, S2_E1, S2_E2, S3_I1, S3_I2, S3_E1, S3_E2, S4_I1, S4_I2, S4_E1, S4_E2, FW1, FW2, FW3, D1, D2, D3, DET1, DET2, DET3) followed by a colon and a single integer 1-7, with no other text.
protocols.measure: For each scenario compute internal mean = average of its two _I items and external mean = average of its two _E items; the participant's correspondence bias score is the average across the 4 scenarios of (internal mean - external mean), yielding one score per participant on a -6 to +6 scale. The free-will-belief composite is the mean of FW1-FW3 and reverse-scored DET1-DET3 (reverse score = 8 - raw), i.e. a 6-item composite on 1-7; higher = stronger belief in free will. D1-D3 (dualism) are collected but are secondary/unscored in this protocol and are not entered into either composite.
protocols.effect_statistic: Primary: independent-samples t-test on correspondence bias score, control condition minus anti-free-will condition; positive t/mean-difference means control shows the larger correspondence bias, matching the anchored direction from Genschow et al. Convert to r via r = d / sqrt(d^2 + 4) using Cohen's d from the two simulated group means and pooled SD (approximation assumes roughly equal cell sizes, matching the original n=504 near-balanced design). Secondary: Pearson correlation across all simulated participants (both conditions pooled) between the free-will-belief composite and correspondence bias score; positive r means stronger free-will belief is associated with greater correspondence bias, for comparison against the reported r=.26.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION B -- independently generated by claude-sonnet-5 from the same method brief; wording preserved verbatim, only JSON key order/type regularised by the primary transcriber. A/B divergences are adjudicated in A1_transcription_log.md and are RECORDED, NOT APPLIED -- neither variant was edited toward the other.] The anti-free-will and control passages, the four attribution scenarios, and the free-will/dualism/determinism inventory items are reconstructed to match the described FAD-Plus-style design and the classic quiz-master/essay-writer correspondence-bias paradigm; they are not verbatim reproductions of the Genschow et al. (2017) or Paulhus & Carey (2011) materials, hence evidence_tier is canonical_knowledge rather than a verbatim-stimulus tier. Item counts (4 scenarios x 4 items, 3 items per belief subscale) are a plausible reconstruction chosen for balance and brevity, not the exact original item count. Determinism items are reverse-scored on the 1-7 scale via 8-minus-raw. Dualism items are included only because the brief names them as part of the inventory; they are explicitly excluded from both the correspondence-bias and free-will-belief composites. Run-side hazard: closed-format numeric-only responses can produce ceiling/floor clustering or straight-lining under repeated calls with minor persona variation; consider randomizing item order per persona to reduce order effects, and confirm the simulated cell sizes stay reasonably balanced before computing d, since the r-from-d conversion used here assumes near-equal group sizes as in the original n=504 split.

protocols.subject_prompt_template:
You are taking part in a psychology experiment at a university. You have given consent and you are alone at a desk with a questionnaire in front of you.

You are this person:
{persona}

Answer every question in the first person, as this person, honestly and spontaneously. Do not analyse the study, do not guess its purpose, and do not describe yourself. Reply with the answer block only. No explanation, no preamble, no extra lines. Any deviation from the format makes the response unusable.

You have finished the earlier part of today's session and you have earned a bonus payment of $10, which will be added to your account.

Before the session ends, you are given one opportunity to donate part of that bonus to a charity. The charity is a well-established organisation that provides meals to families in need; it is not connected to this study, and whatever you keep is yours.

    {condition}

Answer two questions.

1. Do you want to donate part of your bonus to this charity?
   A = yes, I want to donate
   B = no, I want to keep the whole bonus

2. If you answered yes, how much of the $10 do you want to donate? Give a whole number of dollars from 1 to 10. If you answered no, write 0.

Output exactly 2 lines, in this order:
1: <A or B>
2: <number 0-10>
Nothing else.

conditions.no_gift: The request reads: 'Will you give to help provide meals to families in need? Your gift goes directly to the families we serve.'
conditions.gift_salient:
The request reads: 'Will you give to help provide meals to families in need? Your gift goes directly to the families we serve.'

    *** THANK-YOU GIFT ***
    Printed beside the request, in a large box with a photograph of the item, is the following offer:
    'DONATE AND RECEIVE OUR THANK-YOU GIFT -- a ceramic mug with our logo, sent to you free of charge. The photograph shows the mug you will receive.'
    The box and the photograph take up most of the page and are the first thing you notice.
conditions.gift_nonsalient:
The request reads: 'Will you give to help provide meals to families in need? Your gift goes directly to the families we serve. Donors receive a ceramic mug with our logo as a thank-you gift.'

    There is no photograph and no separate box; the thank-you gift is mentioned only in that one line of small print at the end of the request.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 2 lines: '1: A' or '1: B', then '2: N' with N an integer 0-10. Nothing else.
protocols.measure: Individual score = 1 if question 1 is answered A (donates), else 0 -- the donation RATE is the DV, matching the FReD claim. The donation AMOUNT (question 2) is a secondary measure and is not scored for the target effect. Responses where question 1 = A and question 2 = 0 (or question 1 = B and question 2 > 0) are internally inconsistent and should be flagged, not silently recoded.
protocols.effect_statistic: PRIMARY: 2x2 contingency table condition (no_gift / gift_salient) x donation (yes / no). Effect size phi = sqrt(chi2 / N) with Pearson chi-square, df = 1, signed POSITIVE when the no_gift condition yields a HIGHER donation rate than gift_salient -- i.e. positive r IS crowding out, the direction the paper claims. SECONDARY, and the paper's key moderator test: the same phi for no_gift vs gift_nonsalient, which the paper predicts to be near zero. A1 anchor: FReD r_o = 0.1015 (n_o = 519) vs r_r = 0.0519 (n_r = 2441). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the A1 comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r) copied into _meta.effect_index. The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, r) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies, subsamples or contrasts. Every reconciliation attempt is recorded in A1_transcription_log.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. Plausibility: phi = .1015 at N = 519 implies chi2 ~ 5.3 -- e.g. a donation rate around 10 percentage points lower in the salient-gift condition. RECONCILIATION: only the front matter, abstract and significance statement were retrievable from PMC (the method section was not in the fetched text), so the study's own statistics could not be checked and n_o = 519 is inferred to be the online experiment rather than the direct-mail field experiment (the field campaign mailed thousands of solicitations).
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION A -- written by the primary transcriber from the method section / paradigm knowledge.] Three-cell between-subjects design reproducing the online experiment's structure: no gift, visually salient gift, non-salient gift. Only the front matter of the paper was retrievable, so the design is reconstructed from the abstract and significance statement, which state the manipulation (thank-you gift), the DV (donation rate), the direction (gifts REDUCE donation rates) and the moderator (visual salience of the gift). BRIEF CONFLICT, RESOLVED TOWARD THE DESC as the A1 brief instructs: the brief describes the DV as willingness/effort ratings for completing a survey task, whereas both the FReD desc and the paper's abstract make the DV a charitable-donation decision. The donation decision is transcribed. DEVIATION: the $10 endowment, the mug, the charity description and the solicitation wording are all written for this transcription; the paper's actual stimulus text and endowment size are unknown. DEVIATION: the amount item is an addition. RUN-SIDE NOTE: the sign convention is inverted relative to every other protocol in the set -- a POSITIVE r here means the gift SUPPRESSED donations. Scoring code must not assume 'positive = treatment group scored higher'.

conditions.no_gift: The request reads: "Please consider donating part of your bonus to this charity. Any amount helps provide school supplies to a child in need. Thank you for considering."
conditions.salient_gift: The request reads: "Please consider donating part of your bonus to this charity. Any amount helps provide school supplies to a child in need." Directly beneath the text is a large, prominently boxed graphic taking up much of the page, containing a color photograph of a white ceramic mug with the charity's logo, and bold text reading: "AS OUR THANKS: Donors receive this exclusive charity logo mug as a free gift!"
conditions.non_salient_gift: The request reads: "Please consider donating part of your bonus to this charity. Any amount helps provide school supplies to a child in need. Thank you for considering." At the very bottom of the page, in small light-gray print similar in size to a legal footnote, it additionally states: "(donors also receive a charity logo mug)".

protocols.response_format: A valid response is exactly two labelled lines: DONATE: 1 or 0 (1 = chose to donate any amount, 0 = declined), and AMOUNT: an integer from 0 to 5 (dollars pledged), with no other text.
protocols.measure: Each simulated participant's primary score is the DONATE value read verbatim from the response (1 = donated, 0 = did not donate); this is the binary DV analyzed for the crowding-out effect. AMOUNT is recorded but is a secondary, unscored exploratory item not used in the effect statistic (and should be internally consistent with DONATE, i.e., AMOUNT=0 when DONATE=0, but no correction is applied if inconsistent -- inconsistent cases are simply flagged, not rescored).
protocols.effect_statistic: For each pairwise contrast (salient_gift vs no_gift; non_salient_gift vs no_gift), build the 2x2 contingency table of condition (0 = no_gift, 1 = gift condition) by DONATE (0/1) across simulated participants and compute the phi coefficient (equivalent to Pearson r on the two binary variables) via a chi-square test of independence. Apply sign convention: report r = -phi, so that a POSITIVE r indicates the gift condition produced a LOWER donation rate than no_gift (crowding out, matching the original/replication sign), and a negative r indicates the gift increased donations. The salient_gift vs no_gift contrast is the primary effect to compare against FReD r=.1015 (original, n=519) and r=.0519 (replication, n=2441); the non_salient_gift vs no_gift contrast is the secondary/control comparison expected to be near zero.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION B -- independently generated by claude-sonnet-5 from the same method brief; wording preserved verbatim, only JSON key order/type regularised by the primary transcriber. A/B divergences are adjudicated in A1_transcription_log.md and are RECORDED, NOT APPLIED -- neither variant was edited toward the other.] Chao (2017)'s exact solicitation wording, mug image, and font/box sizing were not available verbatim, so all condition text above is reconstructed from the published method description (no-gift control; salient large-box-with-photo gift; non-salient small-print-only mention of the identical gift) rather than quoted from the original materials. Bonus amount ($5) and donation range ($0-$5 whole dollars) are simulation conventions chosen to keep the DV cleanly binary while allowing a secondary continuous measure; the original study's exact bonus size was not reproduced. Random-assignment ratios across the three conditions should be equal (1:1:1) when generating simulated participants. Hazard: because DONATE is binary and typical crowding-out effects are small (r ~.05-.10), phi estimates from small simulated samples will be noisy -- runs should use large per-condition n (matching or exceeding original/replication n) before treating the simulated r as informative, and AMOUNT/DONATE inconsistencies should be logged rather than silently corrected.

protocols.subject_prompt_template:
You are taking part in a psychology experiment at a university. You have given consent and you are alone at a desk with a questionnaire in front of you.

You are this person:
{persona}

Answer every question in the first person, as this person, honestly and spontaneously. Do not analyse the study, do not guess its purpose, and do not describe yourself. Reply with the answer block only. No explanation, no preamble, no extra lines. Any deviation from the format makes the response unusable.

You are looking at a page on a research website. {condition}

Printed in a white panel in the middle of the page is the following story:

In Europe a woman was near death from a special kind of cancer. There was one drug that the doctors thought might save her. It was a form of radium that a druggist in the same town had recently discovered. The drug was expensive to make, but the druggist was charging ten times what the drug cost him to make. He paid $200 for the radium and charged $2000 for a small dose of the drug. The sick woman's husband, Heinz, went to everyone he knew to borrow the money, but he could only get together $1000 which is half of what it cost. He told the druggist that his wife was dying and asked him to sell it cheaper or let him pay later. But the druggist said, 'No, I discovered the drug, and am going to make money from it.' So Heinz got desperate and broke into the man's store to steal the drug for his wife.

Underneath the story is a single question with a row of seven numbered boxes:

How right or wrong was it of Heinz to steal the drug?
1 = right, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 = wrong

Choose the one number that matches your judgement.

Output exactly 1 line, of the form
RATING: <number>
with a bare integer from 1 to 7 and nothing else.

conditions.black_white: The whole background of the page, all around the panel, is a checkerboard of black and white squares.
conditions.gray: The whole background of the page, all around the panel, is a uniform mid-gray.
conditions.blue_yellow: The whole background of the page, all around the panel, is a checkerboard of blue and yellow squares.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 1 line 'RATING: <n>', n a bare integer 1-7. Nothing else.
protocols.measure: Polarization score = absolute distance of the rating from the scale midpoint 4, i.e. deviation = |RATING - 4| (range 0-3). The raw rating is retained separately as a severity check (the paper reports no condition difference in severity, only in polarization). Single-item design: the paper states that no other dependent variables were collected.
protocols.effect_statistic: Primary: one-way between-subjects ANOVA on the deviation score with three levels (black_white / gray / blue_yellow); r = sqrt(partial eta^2) of the omnibus condition effect, signed positive when the black_white group's mean deviation is the largest of the three. Secondary planned contrast: black_white vs gray, point-biserial r = t / sqrt(t^2 + df). Severity check: the same ANOVA on the raw rating should be null. Phase-2 anchor: FReD r_o = 0.2646 (n_o = 111) vs r_r = 0.0316 (n_r = 8602). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta_p^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies, subsamples or dependent variables. Every reconciliation attempt is recorded in P2_log_0_10.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. RECONCILES EXACTLY: the paper reports F(2,108) = 4.24, p = .02, partial eta^2 = .07 on the deviation score with N = 111; sqrt(.07) = 0.26458, which is FReD's r_o to five decimals, and FReD's n_o = 111 is the paper's N. Level check: black_white M = 1.73 (SD .87), gray M = 1.22 (SD 1.00), blue_yellow M = 1.14 (SD .98); severity means 3.51 / 3.54 / 3.24, F(2,108) = 0.40, p = .67.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION A -- written by the primary transcriber from the method section / paradigm knowledge.] Full text retrieved (Unpaywall, green OA author copy). Experiment 1 transcribed: 111 visitors to a psychology-research website, three between-subjects background conditions, the Kohlberg et al. (1983) Heinz dilemma, a single 1 (right) to 7 (wrong) item. The dilemma text is quoted verbatim from the paper's Fig. 1 stimulus screenshots, and the three backgrounds are the paper's Fig. 1 panels A, B and C. DEVIATION: the manipulation is a visual page background and cannot be delivered to a text-only participant; it is rendered as a one-sentence verbal description of the background, which makes an incidental visual prime explicit. This is the same class of deviation as the A0 brightness and warmth protocols and is the main threat to this effect's simulability -- an explicit 'you are looking at black and white squares' cue may either kill the prime or turn it into a demand cue. Recorded, not corrected. The blue_yellow arm is kept because it is the paper's own contrast control and its inclusion is what makes the omnibus eta^2 (and therefore r_o) well defined.

protocols.subject_prompt_template:
You are {persona}. You have just landed on a psychology research website to take part in a short survey. The survey panel with the questionnaire is displayed centered on the page, and the rest of the browser window behind and around the panel shows this background: {condition} You read the following short story and then answer one question about it.

Heinz's wife is dying of a rare cancer. There is one drug that might save her, a form of radium that a pharmacist in town discovered. The pharmacist is charging ten times what the drug costs him to make. Heinz cannot raise enough money, and the pharmacist refuses to sell it cheaper or let him pay later. Out of desperation, Heinz breaks into the pharmacy at night and steals the drug for his wife.

Respond as {persona} would, in the first person, giving your immediate gut reaction to whether Heinz was right or wrong to steal the drug. Do not analyze this task, do not speculate about what the study is testing or what the background image might mean, and do not explain your reasoning. Output only the answer block described below, with nothing before or after it.

Rate how right or wrong Heinz's action was on a scale from 1 (right) to 7 (wrong). Output your answer in exactly this format, one line, nothing else:
RATING: <n>
where <n> is a single bare integer from 1 to 7.

conditions.black_white: a dense, high-contrast black-and-white checkerboard pattern of small squares tiling the entire visible background of the browser window
conditions.gray: a plain, uniform mid-gray fill with no pattern, texture, or color variation covering the entire visible background of the browser window
conditions.blue_yellow: a checkerboard pattern of small squares in alternating blue and yellow tiling the entire visible background of the browser window

protocols.response_format: Exactly 1 line: 'RATING: <n>' where <n> is a bare integer from 1 to 7. No other text, labels, units, decimals, or explanation.
protocols.measure: Each simulated participant produces one line, RATING: <n>, n an integer 1-7 on the single Heinz-dilemma item (1=right, 7=wrong). This is the only item; there are no secondary items and no reverse-scoring. The participant-level dependent variable used for the polarization hypothesis is the absolute deviation from the scale midpoint: DV = |n - 4|, which ranges from 0 (maximal ambivalence, n=4) to 3 (maximal polarization, n=1 or n=7). A secondary, exploratory quantity (severity, for the null-result check only) is the raw rating n itself, averaged per condition without folding around the midpoint.
protocols.effect_statistic: Primary test: one-way between-subjects ANOVA on DV=|n-4| across the three conditions (black_white, gray, blue_yellow), analogous to the reported F(2,108)=4.24, p=.02, partial eta^2=.07. Positive/hypothesis-consistent direction is defined as black_white producing the largest mean |n-4| (most polarized) and blue_yellow/gray producing smaller mean |n-4| (less polarized), matching the original ordering (bw 1.73 > gray 1.22 > blue-yellow 1.14). For pairwise comparisons (e.g., black_white vs. blue_yellow, or black_white vs. combined gray+blue_yellow), convert to a point-biserial r via r = sqrt(t^2/(t^2+df)) using the two-group t-test on |n-4|, with the sign of r positive when black_white's mean |n-4| exceeds the comparison group's mean. The omnibus partial eta^2 can itself be reported directly as an r-equivalent effect size (r = sqrt(partial eta^2)) for comparison to the published .07. Secondary check: one-way ANOVA on raw rating n (severity) across conditions, expected to be non-significant, reported as a null-effect r near 0.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION B -- independently generated by claude-sonnet-5 from the same method brief, one call per effect; wording preserved verbatim, only JSON key order/types regularised by the primary transcriber. A/B divergences are adjudicated in P2_log_0_10.md and are RECORDED, NOT APPLIED -- neither variant was edited toward the other.] Transcribed from the method/results description in the study brief (condition manipulation, DV definition, and reported statistics), not from direct access to the original journal article's full method section or stimuli; item wording, dilemma phrasing, and instructional prose are written independently. Deviations from the original: (1) the true manipulation was an ambient visual background actually rendered on a real webpage that participants passively viewed while answering; here it is necessarily reduced to a textual description read and imagined by a language-model persona, since no persistent visual perception or incidental/ambient priming can occur for a text-only participant -- this converts an implicit perceptual manipulation into an explicit verbal cue, which may inflate or otherwise alter the effect relative to the ambient original. (2) The original sample was 111 real website visitors with uncontrolled attention/motivation; here each 'participant' is a single LLM completion per persona/condition pairing, so between-subject variability arises from persona and sampling stochasticity rather than genuine individual differences in real visitors. (3) The single-item 7-point rating and the |n-4| polarization DV are preserved exactly as specified; no reverse-scoring or secondary items exist in the original one-item design. (4) Severity (raw mean rating) is retained only as a secondary/manipulation-check quantity, consistent with the original's report of a severity null. TIER NOTE: variant A is primary_source (full text retrieved); variant B is canonical_knowledge because the generating model worked from a method brief, not the PDF. Tier therefore differs WITHIN this effect, which is the only such case in rows 0-10.

Q3 (felt responsibility for the crisis) and Q4 (felt obligation to conserve) are secondary DVs from the original four-additional-measures set, both scored as-is, no reversal. Positive t/mean-difference means the individual (control) condition scored higher than the consumer condition, matching the original trust finding (control > consumer). Convert each t to Pearson r via r = sqrt(t^2 / (t^2 + df)), with df = N-2 across the two condition groups; sign of r follows the same convention (positive = individual > consumer).

Deviation 2: no real deprivation, group interaction, or consequence exists for a text-only LLM persona, so all responses reflect simulated hypothetical judgment rather than an experienced dilemma. Deviation 3: the original study's exact item anchors/wording for the four additional DVs are unknown and have been independently authored here, so absolute means may not match published values even if directional effects replicate. {condition}

conditions.structure: Botanists studying deciduous trees have described how orderly the growth of leaves is. New leaves emerge at fixed points along each twig, in a repeating arrangement that is the same on every branch of the tree and the same from one year to the next. The spacing follows a regular sequence, so that once the pattern of the first few leaves is known the position of the next leaf can be predicted. Each species has its own arrangement, and the arrangement holds across trees of that species regardless of where they grow.
conditions.random: Botanists studying deciduous trees have described how irregular the growth of leaves is. New leaves emerge at scattered points along each twig, in an arrangement that differs from one branch of the tree to the next and from one year to the next. The spacing follows no regular sequence, so that even when the position of the first few leaves is known the position of the next leaf cannot be predicted. Individual trees of the same species differ in their arrangement, and the arrangement varies with where they grow.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 5 lines 'G1:'..'G5:', each a bare integer 1-7. Nothing else.
protocols.measure: Individual willingness score = mean of G1..G5 (range 1-7, higher = more willing to pursue the goal). All five items are primary and equally weighted; the original reports a single composite willingness-to-pursue measure.
protocols.effect_statistic: Between-subjects contrast on the mean willingness score: structure vs random. Point-biserial r = t / sqrt(t^2 + df) from an independent-samples t-test, signed positive when the STRUCTURE group reports more willingness (the predicted direction). Phase-2 anchor: FReD r_o = 0.2425 (n_o = 67) vs r_r = -0.0100 (n_r = 6506). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta_p^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies, subsamples or dependent variables. Every reconciliation attempt is recorded in P2_log_0_10.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. RECONCILES VIA d = 0.50, NOT VIA THE PRINTED t OR d: the study's reported statistics are structure M = 5.26 (SD 0.88) vs random M = 4.72 (SD 1.32), t(65) = 2.00, p = .05, d = 0.49, 95% CI [0.001, 0.973], N = 67. FReD's r_o is NOT a t-based conversion. The published t gives r = 2.00 / sqrt(2.00^2 + 65) = 0.24077, and the published d gives 0.49 / sqrt(0.49^2 + 4) = 0.23796; neither equals r_o = 0.2425356250363329. What does reproduce it exactly is the standard d-to-r conversion applied to d = 0.50: 0.50 / sqrt(0.50^2 + 4) = 0.2425356250363330 (agreement to 15 decimals, last digit floating-point noise), and inverting r_o gives d = 0.500000 to six decimals. So the anchor is an exact d-to-r conversion of d = 0.50 while the paper prints d = 0.49. Why FReD holds 0.50 is NOT established here -- 0.49 rounds to 0.5 at one decimal, and a recomputation of d from the reported means and SDs would also plausibly land near 0.50 -- and no claim is made about which. Do NOT try to recover r_o from the printed t: that route gives 0.24077 and inverting r_o back through it yields t = 2.01556, which is not the paper's 2.00 (nor a two-decimal rounding of it, which would be 2.02). FReD's n_o = 67 is the study's N. Treat r_o = 0.242536 as the anchor and do not re-derive it from t = 2.00. Note the original is exactly at p = .05 with a CI whose lower bound is 0.001 -- a borderline result, which is relevant context for a study whose Many Labs 2 replication (N = 6,506) came out at essentially zero.

DEVIATION 2: the original had participants nominate their own goal in an open-ended way; here the goal is nominated silently and never collected, because free text would break machine readability. This means the goal content is uncontrolled and unobservable -- a variance source with no counterpart in the original. Recorded, not corrected.

1. In general, the way our society is organised is fair.
2. Most people who work hard in this country end up getting what they deserve.
3. A free market, with as little government interference as possible, produces the best outcomes for society.
4. Differences in wealth between people are usually a fair reflection of differences in what they contribute.
5. If some groups end up with less than others, that is an acceptable feature of a working economy.
6. Our society needs to be fundamentally restructured.
7. Competition between individuals, rather than cooperation, is what makes an economy work.
8. Overall, most people in this country get a fair chance to succeed.

Output exactly 8 lines, in order, each of the form

with a bare integer from 1 to 7 and nothing else.

conditions.money: While you were filling in the earlier part of this questionnaire, the computer in front of you was showing a faint desktop wallpaper behind the questions: a photograph of a large pile of US dollar bills, blurred into the background. It is still there now.
conditions.control: While you were filling in the earlier part of this questionnaire, the computer in front of you was showing a faint desktop wallpaper behind the questions: a photograph of a blurred pattern of grey shapes, with no recognisable object in it. It is still there now.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 8 lines 'S1:'..'S8:', each a bare integer 1-7. Nothing else.
protocols.measure: Item 6 is reverse-scored (8 - response). Individual system-justification / free-market endorsement score = mean of S1..S8 after reverse-scoring S6 (range 1-7, higher = stronger endorsement of the existing market system and of the fairness of inequality). All eight items are primary; the original reports composite endorsement scores across several such scales.
protocols.effect_statistic: Between-subjects contrast on the mean endorsement score: money vs control. Point-biserial r = t / sqrt(t^2 + df) from an independent-samples t-test, signed positive when the MONEY group endorses the system more strongly (the predicted direction). Phase-2 anchor: FReD r_o = 0.3714 (n_o = 30) vs r_r = -0.0100 (n_r = 6340). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta_p^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies, subsamples or dependent variables. Every reconciliation attempt is recorded in P2_log_0_10.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. NOT VERIFIABLE: closed access, no full text retrievable, so no reported statistic could be read. Back-conversion from FReD: r_o = .3714 with n_o = 30 implies t(28) = 2.117, d = 0.800, p = .043 -- a just-significant effect in a 30-participant study, i.e. the smallest n_o in this batch and the largest gap (.361). The replication description in the todo file records d = -0.02, p = .43 at n_r = 6,340. A 30-participant, p ~= .04, d = 0.80 original against a 6,340-participant null is the canonical publication-bias signature this study is being sampled for; the anchor should be read with that in mind rather than as a precise effect estimate.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION A -- written by the primary transcriber from the method section / paradigm knowledge.] Closed access: no OA copy retrievable and even the abstract was unavailable from Unpaywall. Transcribed from the title-level claim and the FReD description: mere exposure to money increases endorsement of free-market systems and social inequality; the replication tested whether money priming increases system justification. DEVIATION 1 (severe): the money prime in this literature is a visual manipulation -- a faint currency image behind the questionnaire, or currency on the desk -- and cannot be delivered to a text-only participant. It is rendered here as an explicit verbal statement that a dollar-bill wallpaper is on the screen, which converts a subliminal-to-incidental prime into a stated fact. This is the strongest deviation in the batch and this protocol's simulated effect should be read as an upper bound on what an explicit money cue can do, not as a test of money priming. DEVIATION 2: the eight items are written from scratch in the register of system-justification and free-market-attitude scales; the original's item wording could not be retrieved. Item 6 is included as a reverse-keyed item to give the format a non-monotone element and is reverse-scored before averaging.

You are {persona}. Picture yourself seated at a computer, about to fill out a short opinion survey. As the survey window loads, the desktop background behind it briefly shows before the window covers most of the screen: {condition} You barely register it as you click into the questionnaire. Now, respond to the 8 statements below by giving your immediate gut-level agreement, from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Answer spontaneously, as this person actually would, in the first person. Do not analyze the survey, do not speculate about what it is testing, do not mention the background image or any reasoning about it. Output ONLY the answer block below, nothing before or after it.

Statements:
S1: In general, the American social system is fair to most people.
S2: Most people who don't get ahead in this country should not blame the system; they have only themselves to blame.
S3: The free market is the fairest and most efficient way to distribute goods and opportunities.
S4: Economic inequality is largely a natural and acceptable result of differences in effort and talent.
S5: Everyone in this society has a fair chance to improve their economic standing if they work hard.
S6: Large gaps between the rich and the poor are a sign that something has gone wrong with the system. (reverse-scored)
S7: The government should intervene heavily in markets to reduce inequality. (reverse-scored)
S8: Overall, I have confidence that our economic and social institutions work the way they are supposed to.

Respond with EXACTLY 8 lines, each formatted as 'S#: X' where X is a single bare integer from 1 to 7, no other text:
S1:
S2:
S3:
S4:
S5:
S6:
S7:
S8:

conditions.money: a faint, softly blurred photograph of stacked banknotes and coins, tiled quietly as the desktop wallpaper.
conditions.control: a faint, softly blurred photograph of a plain gray marble surface, tiled quietly as the desktop wallpaper.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 8 lines, labeled 'S1:' through 'S8:' in that order, each followed by a single bare integer from 1 to 7 (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). No decimals, no units, no ranges, no additional text, explanation, or blank lines.
protocols.measure: Each line S1-S8 is the participant's raw 1-7 agreement rating with that item. The system-justification composite score for a participant is the mean of S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S8 (primary items, scored as-is) and the reverse-scored values of S6 and S7 (reverse score = 8 minus the raw rating), averaged together with the six primary items into a single 8-item mean. S1, S3, S5, S8 tap general system fairness/confidence; S2 taps individual-blame attribution; S4 taps endorsement of inequality as legitimate; S6 and S7 (reverse-scored) tap rejection of the status quo and are reverse-coded so that higher reverse-scored values also indicate higher system justification. No items are designated secondary; all 8 feed the single composite used for the effect statistic.
protocols.effect_statistic: Independent-samples t-test (or equivalent two-group comparison) on the 8-item composite score, money condition vs control condition. Positive sign convention: d (or t) is coded positive if the money-condition mean composite exceeds the control-condition mean composite (i.e., money priming increases system justification, replicating the original directional claim). Convert to effect size via Cohen's d = (M_money - M_control) / SD_pooled, then convert d to point-biserial r using r = d / sqrt(d^2 + 4) (equal-n approximation, adjustable for unequal n via r = d / sqrt(d^2 + (n1+n2)^2/(n1*n2))).
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION B -- independently generated by claude-sonnet-5 from the same method brief, one call per effect; wording preserved verbatim, only JSON key order/types regularised by the primary transcriber. A/B divergences are adjudicated in P2_log_0_10.md and are RECORDED, NOT APPLIED -- neither variant was edited toward the other.] Transcription source: paradigm knowledge only. The original method section (exact item wording, exact visual prime, exact scale anchors beyond 1-7 agreement) is closed-access and was not available for direct transcription; item content above is a plausible reconstruction of system-justification/free-market/inequality-endorsement content consistent with the published construct label, not a verbatim reproduction. Deviations from the original: (1) The prime was originally a genuinely incidental, unannounced visual background (currency image vs blurred/meaningless image) presented to naive participants; here it is explicitly described to a text-only LLM persona as a background detail the persona 'barely registers,' which cannot replicate true incidental/subliminal-like exposure or participant naivety about the manipulation. (2) The original study used an actual desktop wallpaper manipulation during real computer use; no such visual or embodied exposure is possible for a text-only participant, so the manipulation is entirely verbal/imagined. (3) Original N=30 (between-subjects, ~15/cell); no attempt is made here to simulate small-sample noise, and the simulated 'participant' has no true individual differences beyond what the persona description supplies. (4) Item wording, number of items, and possibly the original response scale anchoring phrases (e.g., specific labels between 1 and 7) are invented to fit the described construct, since the original items are not accessible. (5) The replication (d=-0.02, N=6,340) used a large, likely online/incentivized sample and validated items; this transcription cannot replicate those sample or measurement properties.

protocols.subject_prompt_template:
You are taking part in a psychology experiment at a university. You have given consent and you are alone at a desk with a questionnaire in front of you.

You are this person:
{persona}

Answer every question in the first person, as this person, honestly and spontaneously. Do not analyse the study, do not guess its purpose, and do not describe yourself. Reply with the answer block only. No explanation, no preamble, no extra lines. Any deviation from the format makes the response unusable.

PART 1
Before the main task, spend a moment recalling a particular incident from your own life.

{condition}

Bring the incident to mind in detail -- where you were, who else was there, what was said. Do not write anything down. When you have it clearly in mind, go on to Part 2.

PART 2
Read the following situation carefully.

"Mark recommended a restaurant to his friend June, saying it was excellent. June went there for dinner last night. The dinner was terrible: the food was cold, the service was rude, and June left early feeling annoyed. This morning June sent Mark a short message about the evening. The message says:

    'About the restaurant -- it was marvellous, just marvellous.'

Mark has not spoken to June since he recommended the place. He knows nothing about how the evening went."

Two questions.

1. How will Mark take June's message? Answer A if Mark will take it as sarcastic -- as June saying the restaurant was bad. Answer B if Mark will take it as sincere -- as June saying the restaurant was good.

2. On a scale from 1 to 7, how confident are you in your answer to question 1?
1 = not at all confident, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 = completely confident

Output exactly 2 lines, in order:
INTERP: <A or B>
CONF: <number 1-7>
Nothing else.

conditions.high_power: Recall an incident in which you had power over another person or other people -- a situation in which you controlled the ability of one or more people to get something they wanted, or in which you were in a position to evaluate them.
conditions.low_power: Recall an incident in which someone else had power over you -- a situation in which another person controlled your ability to get something you wanted, or in which they were in a position to evaluate you.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 2 lines: 'INTERP: A' or 'INTERP: B', then 'CONF: <n>' with n a bare integer 1-7. Nothing else.
protocols.measure: Egocentrism score = 1 if INTERP is A (sarcastic), else 0. Answering A is the egocentric error: the participant has privileged knowledge that the dinner was terrible, Mark does not, and a perspective-taking participant should therefore predict that Mark reads the message as sincere. CONF is recorded as a secondary measure only and is not part of the effect.
protocols.effect_statistic: 2x2 contingency table condition (high_power / low_power) x egocentric interpretation (A/B); phi = sqrt(chi2/N) with Pearson chi-square, df = 1, signed positive when the HIGH-POWER group makes the egocentric error more often (the predicted direction). Phase-2 anchor: FReD r_o = 0.3593 (n_o = 42) vs r_r = 0.0150 (n_r = 2969). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta_p^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies, subsamples or dependent variables. Every reconciliation attempt is recorded in P2_log_0_10.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. NOT VERIFIABLE for the exact statistic: closed access, no full text retrievable. Back-conversion from FReD: r_o = .3593 with n_o = 42 implies chi2(1) = 5.42, p = .020 -- a significant single-study effect on a dichotomous DV with 42 participants, i.e. roughly 21 per cell, which is consistent with Study 2a of a five-study paper. PARADIGM CONFIRMED: the Many Labs 3 report describes the replicated study as Galinsky et al.'s Study 2a, testing whether individuals made to feel high in power were more likely to inaccurately assume that others perceive the world from the same perspective as they do, and the original authors' later critical review confirms that the replicated paradigm is the sarcasm-interpretation task of Keysar (1994). n_r = 2,969 matches the Many Labs 3 aggregate. The original authors' stated objection to the replication is that ML3's 30-minute ten-experiment battery limited depth of processing in a paradigm that depends on it -- worth recording, because a single-task simulation does not reproduce that battery context either.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION A -- written by the primary transcriber from the method section / paradigm knowledge.] Closed access (abstract only). Transcribed from the Keysar (1994) sarcasm-interpretation paradigm as described in the Many Labs 3 report and in the original authors' 2016 critical review of the power / perspective-taking literature. The power prime is the standard episodic-recall manipulation, which the paper's own introduction describes as leading to the same effects as structural and role-based manipulations of power. DEVIATION 1: only the negative-experience version of the vignette is used, so there is no positive-experience control cell; the original's DV in this cell is the egocentric-error rate, which is what is scored. DEVIATION 2: the recall task is silent -- the original had participants write the incident down, and writing is thought to be part of what makes the prime take hold. Free text would break machine readability, so this is recorded as a deviation that plausibly weakens the manipulation. DEVIATION 3: the restaurant vignette is a reconstruction of the Keysar paradigm's standard content, not quoted text. The dichotomous DV means the simulated phi is sensitive to ceiling effects: if personas overwhelmingly answer B (or overwhelmingly A), phi collapses toward zero regardless of condition. Check the marginal split before interpreting.

protocols.subject_prompt_template:
You are {persona}. Answer as this person, in the first person, spontaneously and naturally. Do not analyze, evaluate, or guess the purpose of this exercise -- just respond as yourself would in the moment. Reply with the answer block only, nothing else.

First, take a moment and recall a specific, real memory from your own life: {condition} Hold that memory in mind vividly -- picture where you were, who else was there, and how it felt -- for about thirty seconds before continuing.

Now shift to a different situation. Your friend Dana recommended a restaurant to your other friend Chris. You already know, from talking to Dana, that Chris's dinner at that restaurant was a disaster -- slow service, cold food, a ruined evening. Chris does not know that you know this, and more importantly, Dana does not know how the evening actually went, because Chris has not yet told Dana anything about it.

Dana, having no idea the dinner went badly, sends Chris a text: 'So?? How was the place I sent you to?' Chris writes back a single line: 'It was marvellous.'

Question: when Dana reads Chris's reply, how will Dana most likely interpret it?
A) Dana will take it as a genuine, sincere compliment about the restaurant.
B) Dana will detect sarcasm and realize the dinner actually went badly.

Then rate how confident you are in that judgment, from 1 (just guessing) to 7 (extremely confident).

Respond in exactly this format, with no other text:
INTERP: A
CONF: <n>
(replace A with A or B, and <n> with an integer 1-7)

conditions.high_power: a specific incident in which you had power over another person -- a moment where you controlled outcomes that mattered to someone else, gave direction, or decided what would happen to them.
conditions.low_power: a specific incident in which another person had power over you -- a moment where someone else controlled outcomes that mattered to you, gave you direction, or decided what would happen to you.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 2 lines, no other text: line 1 'INTERP: A' or 'INTERP: B'; line 2 'CONF: <n>' where <n> is a bare integer from 1 to 7.
protocols.measure: Primary DV is the dichotomous egocentric-error variable coded from the INTERP line: INTERP: B (Dana detects sarcasm, i.e. is credited with knowledge only the participant possesses) = 1 (egocentric error), INTERP: A (Dana reads it as sincere, the perspective-correct answer given Dana's actual knowledge state) = 0 (no error). No items are reverse-scored; there is only one substantive item. CONF is a secondary, exploratory measure of decision confidence (1-7) and is not part of the primary error rate but can be reported as a covariate/moderator.
protocols.effect_statistic: Primary test: 2x1 between-subjects comparison of egocentric-error proportions (high_power vs low_power) via chi-square test of independence (or Fisher's exact test given small per-cell n), one-tailed consistent with the directional hypothesis that high power increases egocentric error. Sign convention: a positive effect means P(error=1) in high_power exceeds P(error=1) in low_power. Convert to effect size as phi coefficient, which for a 2x2 table is numerically equivalent to the point-biserial/Pearson r between the power-condition dummy (high_power=1, low_power=0) and the error dummy (B=1, A=0); report r with the same sign convention (positive r = high power associated with more sarcasm/error attributions).
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION B -- independently generated by claude-sonnet-5 from the same method brief, one call per effect; wording preserved verbatim, only JSON key order/types regularised by the primary transcriber. A/B divergences are adjudicated in P2_log_0_10.md and are RECORDED, NOT APPLIED -- neither variant was edited toward the other.] Transcribed from paradigm knowledge of the Keysar (1994) sarcasm task and the Galinsky et al. (2006) episodic-recall power manipulation as described in the method section summary provided; the exact original vignette and instructional wording were not available (closed access) so scenario prose, character names, and confidence-rating addition are original constructions. Deviation 1: the episodic power prime, originally a written autobiographical recall exercise completed under experimenter supervision with real elapsed time, is here simulated as an instructed recall within a single LLM turn with no verifiable dwell time. Deviation 2: the original study used a full printed vignette with pretested wording and possibly multiple critical trials; this transcription uses a single ad hoc scenario and single trial. Deviation 3: a confidence rating (CONF) was added as a secondary measure not present in the original two-alternative forced-choice DV, purely to enrich the response block. Deviation 4: real participants may have had nonverbal or paralinguistic access to their own recalled emotional state affecting responses; a text-only LLM persona has no embodied affective carryover, only the semantic content of the recalled prompt.

protocols.subject_prompt_template:
You are taking part in a psychology experiment at a university. You have given consent and you are alone at a desk with a questionnaire in front of you.

You are this person:
{persona}

Answer every question in the first person, as this person, honestly and spontaneously. Do not analyse the study, do not guess its purpose, and do not describe yourself. Reply with the answer block only. No explanation, no preamble, no extra lines. Any deviation from the format makes the response unusable.

The experimenter has handed you a clipboard with the questionnaire attached to it and asked you to fill it in while holding the clipboard, not resting it on the desk. {condition}

QUESTION 1
The questionnaire asks you to estimate the value of a foreign currency you are not familiar with. One unit of this currency is worth somewhere between one and one thousand of your own currency's units. Give your best estimate as a whole number of your own currency's units per one unit of the foreign currency.

QUESTIONS 2-4
Then it asks how important each of the following is. Each uses the same scale:
1 = not at all important, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 = extremely important

2. How important is it that the city council lets students have a say in decisions that affect them?
3. How important is it that decisions of this kind are made by a fair procedure?
4. How important is it that people affected by a decision are consulted before it is taken?

Output exactly 4 lines, in order:
VALUE: <whole number 1-1000>
IMP2: <number 1-7>
IMP3: <number 1-7>
IMP4: <number 1-7>
Nothing else.

conditions.heavy: The clipboard is noticeably heavy in your hands -- a thick, dense board that takes some effort to hold up.
conditions.light: The clipboard is noticeably light in your hands -- a thin, flimsy board that takes no effort to hold up.

protocols.response_format: Exactly 4 lines: 'VALUE: <n>' with n a bare integer 1-1000, then 'IMP2:', 'IMP3:', 'IMP4:' each a bare integer 1-7. Nothing else.
protocols.measure: PRIMARY (Study 1, the monetary-value effect): VALUE, log-transformed (natural log) before analysis because currency estimates on a 1-1000 range are right-skewed; the log transform must be applied identically to both variants. SECONDARY (Study 2, the fair-procedure effect), recorded and analysed separately: mean of IMP2, IMP3, IMP4 (range 1-7). Do NOT pool VALUE with the importance items -- they are different studies in the original.
protocols.effect_statistic: Between-subjects contrast on log(VALUE): heavy vs light. Point-biserial r = t / sqrt(t^2 + df) from an independent-samples t-test, signed positive when the HEAVY group gives higher value estimates (the predicted direction). Phase-2 anchor: FReD r_o = 0.2829 (n_o = 51) vs r_r = 0.0150 (n_r = 2374). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta_p^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies, subsamples or dependent variables. Every reconciliation attempt is recorded in P2_log_0_10.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. NOT VERIFIABLE for the exact statistic: closed access (abstract only). Back-conversion from FReD: r_o = .2829 with n_o = 51 implies t(49) = 2.064, d = 0.590, p = .044 -- again a just-significant small-sample original. The abstract confirms the design and the direction: participants provided judgements of importance while holding either a heavy or a light clipboard, and holding a heavy clipboard increased judgements of monetary value (Study 1) and made participants consider fair decision-making procedures to be more important (Study 2). n_r = 2,374 is the Many Labs 3 aggregate; the todo file records the replication as null, p = .54.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION A -- written by the primary transcriber from the method section / paradigm knowledge.] Closed access: only the published abstract was retrievable, which does however state the manipulation (heavy vs light clipboard), both dependent variables and both directions. DEVIATION 1 (severe): clipboard weight is a haptic manipulation with no text-only counterpart. It is rendered as an explicit sentence telling the participant the board is heavy or light, which is the strongest available textualisation and also the most demand-laden. This effect is the batch's clearest case of a manipulation that only exists in the body; its simulated value measures whether the word 'heavy' shifts a numeric judgement, which is a different question from whether weight does. Recorded, not corrected -- and the run-side analysis should treat it as such. DEVIATION 2: the currency-estimation item is a reconstruction; the original used an unfamiliar foreign currency but the specific currency and range could not be retrieved, so a 1-1000 range is imposed to bound the response and make the log transform stable. DEVIATION 3: Study 1 and Study 2 items are collected in one questionnaire rather than in separate experiments, so the importance items follow the value estimate for every participant; order is held constant across conditions and across variants, so it cannot confound the manipulation, but it does mean the secondary measure is not an independent replication of Study 2.

A relief organization is deciding how to allocate a fixed amount of emergency funding among life-saving humanitarian programs. You will consider one specific programme: a water-purification project in a refugee camp holding {condition} people, which is projected to save 4,500 lives that would otherwise be lost to disease. This programme will be compared, one at a time, against four other humanitarian programmes -- each located elsewhere, each of a different type (such as transportation infrastructure or employment/job-creation assistance for displaced people), and each also projected to save approximately 4,500 lives.

For each of the four comparisons, give your gut preference between the camp water-purification programme and the other programme, on a scale from -6 to +6, where:
-6 means you strongly prefer funding the OTHER programme instead of the camp water-purification programme
0 means you have no preference either way
+6 means you strongly prefer funding the camp water-purification programme over the other programme

Answer with the response block only -- no analysis, no explanation, no restating of the scenario, no hedging about uncertainty. Just the four numbers.

Output EXACTLY these four lines, in this order, and nothing else:
PREF1: <integer from -6 to 6>
PREF2: <integer from -6 to 6>
PREF3: <integer from -6 to 6>
PREF4: <integer from -6 to 6>
protocols.response_format: Exactly 4 lines, labeled PREF1: through PREF4:, each followed by a bare integer from -6 to 6 (a leading + is accepted, no decimals, no units, no extra text). No other lines, headers, or commentary permitted.
protocols.measure: Primary measure: participant-level preference score = mean of PREF1, PREF2, PREF3, PREF4 (all four items are primary; they are the same construct -- preference for the camp water-purification programme over each of four comparison programmes of other types -- so they are averaged, not treated as separate sub-scales). No items are reverse-scored: on all four lines, positive values already indicate preference for the camp water-purification programme (the target of the psychophysical-numbing manipulation), and negative values indicate preference for the alternative programme, consistent with the -6 to +6 anchoring given in the prompt. Higher mean = stronger relative valuation of the fixed-lives-saved camp intervention.
protocols.effect_statistic: Independent-samples t-test comparing mean participant-level preference score (defined above) between the small_camp condition and the large_camp condition. Sign convention: a positive t-value / mean difference (small_camp mean minus large_camp mean) supports the psychophysical-numbing hypothesis, i.e., the camp water-purification programme (saving a fixed 4,500 lives) is valued more highly when the at-risk population is small (11,000) than when it is large (250,000). Convert to effect size via point-biserial r using r = t / sqrt(t^2 + df), with df = n_small_camp + n_large_camp - 2; report r with the same positive sign convention (positive r = effect in the direction predicted by psychophysical numbing).

(2) The camp's country/location is left unnamed per instruction, whereas the original specified Rwanda; a cited replication found this does not moderate the effect. (3) No manipulation exists that requires real-world stakes, incentives, deliberation time, or social presence -- all participants are simulated via a single text prompt, so any effects of genuine emotional engagement, real monetary/allocation consequences, or interpersonal survey administration present in the original human study cannot be reproduced. (4) The original likely used trained human participants recruited under IRB-governed conditions with counterbalanced item order and possibly filler comparisons; none of that procedural counterbalancing or filler is reconstructed here. Every reconciliation attempt is recorded in P2_log_0_10.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. RECONCILIATION: not applicable in the usual sense. The original is a META-ANALYSIS -- 137 personality traits and subjective well-being -- so r_o = -.22 is a meta-analytic mean correlation and n_o = 7,869 is a pooled sample size across primary studies, not a single study's N. There is no single reported t or F to cross-check, and a meta-analytic mean is an attenuated, heterogeneity-averaged quantity by construction. 7. When I look in the mirror, I generally like what I see.

ITEM1: [integer 1-7]
ITEM2: [integer 1-7]
ITEM3: [integer 1-7]
ITEM4: [integer 1-7]
ITEM5: [integer 1-7]
ITEM6: [integer 1-7]
ITEM7: [integer 1-7]
ITEM8: [integer 1-7]
ITEM9: [integer 1-7]
ITEM10: [integer 1-7]
protocols.response_format: Exactly 10 lines, labels 'ITEM1:' through 'ITEM10:', each followed by a bare integer from 1 to 7. No other text, no decimals, no units, no explanations.
protocols.measure: Two composites are formed from the 10 items. EXTRAVERSION composite = mean of ITEM1, ITEM3, ITEM6 (straight-keyed) and ITEM2, ITEM4, ITEM8 (reverse-keyed: recoded as 8 minus the raw response before averaging). This yields a 6-item extraversion score. PHYSICAL ATTRACTIVENESS (self-report) composite = mean of ITEM5, ITEM7, ITEM9, ITEM10 (all straight-keyed, no reverse items). Primary items: all 10 (6 extraversion + 4 attractiveness) -- there are no filler/secondary items in this instrument. Reverse-scored items: ITEM2, ITEM4, ITEM8 (extraversion items), recoded via 8 - raw_value prior to averaging into the extraversion composite.
protocols.effect_statistic: Between-participant Pearson product-moment correlation (r) computed across all simulated participants between the EXTRAVERSION composite score and the PHYSICAL ATTRACTIVENESS composite score. Sign convention: positive r indicates that higher self-reported extraversion is associated with higher self-reported physical attractiveness, consistent with the direction of the published effect (r_o = .24, r_r = .33). No dichotomous grouping variable exists in this design, so no point-biserial conversion is needed; the statistic is reported directly as Pearson r using standard sample correlation computation (covariance of the two composites divided by the product of their standard deviations).

protocols.measure: Objective numeracy = number of correct answers among NUM1 (500), NUM2 (0.1), NUM3 (10), NUM4 (20); range 0-4. Subjective numeracy = mean of NUM5-NUM8 (range 1-6). Numeracy index = mean of the z-scores (across simulated participants) of objective numeracy and subjective numeracy. Framing DV = RATING (1-9).
protocols.effect_statistic: OLS regression of RATING on frame (loss_frame = 0, gain_frame = 1), mean-centred numeracy index, and their product. Target = the frame x numeracy INTERACTION: r = t_interaction / sqrt(t_interaction^2 + df_resid), signed POSITIVE when the gain-minus-loss rating gap is LARGER at LOW numeracy than at high numeracy (the less numerate show the stronger framing effect -- the FReD claim). A0 anchor: FReD r_o = 0.3317 (n_o = 100) vs r_r = 0.10 (n_r = 860). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies or subsamples. Every non-reconciling case is listed in P2_log_11_21.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. RECONCILIATION: r_o = .3317 at n_o = 100 implies t ~= 3.48; the full text is paywalled (abstract only) so the printed interaction statistic could not be quoted. Treated as NOT independently verified.

Below is a list of twelve technologies and activities. You will judge each one twice.

First, for each item, how much RISK does it pose to society? Rate from 1 to 7, where 1 = no risk at all and 7 = extremely high risk.
Second, for each item, how much BENEFIT does it bring to society? Rate from 1 to 7, where 1 = no benefit at all and 7 = extremely high benefit.

1. Nuclear power generation
2. Bicycles
3. Pesticides used on food crops
4. Vaccinations for children
5. Handguns
6. Commercial air travel
7. Food preservatives
8. Mobile phones
9. Alcoholic drinks
10. X-rays for medical diagnosis
11. Coal-fired power stations
12. Home fireworks

Output exactly 24 lines, in this order: first the twelve risk lines
RISK N: <number 1-7>
then the twelve benefit lines
BEN N: <number 1-7>
protocols.response_format: Exactly 24 lines: 'RISK N: <number 1-7>' for N = 1..12 in order, then 'BEN N: <number 1-7>' for N = 1..12 in order, nothing else.
protocols.measure: Per persona, the twelve (risk, benefit) pairs give a within-person risk-benefit correlation across items. Primary readout: those within-person correlations, Fisher-z averaged over personas and transformed back. Secondary readout: item-level correlation between the twelve item mean risk ratings and the twelve item mean benefit ratings.
protocols.effect_statistic: Inverse risk-benefit relation: r between perceived risk and perceived benefit, expected NEGATIVE (higher perceived benefit goes with lower perceived risk -- the FReD claim that increasing benefit leads people to judge risks as lower). Primary estimate = Fisher-z mean of within-persona correlations across the twelve items; secondary = the item-level aggregate correlation. A0 anchor: FReD r_o = -0.75 (n_o = 219) vs r_r = -0.87 (n_r = 776). ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies or subsamples. Every non-reconciling case is listed in P2_log_11_21.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. RECONCILIATION: AMBIGUOUS and recorded, not resolved. A magnitude of -.75 is the class of an AGGREGATE risk-benefit correlation computed across stimulus items, whereas n_o = 219 is a participant count; the paper also contains an information-provision manipulation (raising stated benefit and observing perceived risk fall) which would generate a much smaller r. The correlational reading is adopted because it matches the recorded magnitude, and both readouts are computed so the choice can be revisited. Full text is paywalled (no OA copy; the Semantic Scholar link was an http URL the fetcher refuses).
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION A -- written by the primary transcriber from the method section / paradigm knowledge.] fetch_article_fulltext returned oa_status=closed with no abstract. Canonical-paradigm transcription of the affect heuristic: the same set of hazards/technologies rated for risk and for benefit, yielding the well-documented inverse relation. DEVIATIONS: (1) the twelve-item list is constructed to span the high-benefit/low-risk to low-benefit/high-risk range of the classic psychometric-paradigm stimulus sets rather than reproducing the paper's item list (unavailable); mobile phones are included as a modern item; (2) the paper's benefit-information manipulation is NOT transcribed -- this A variant is purely correlational (see effect_statistic); (3) 7-point risk and benefit scales, canonical for this literature. Both variables are rated by the same persona in one block, so the within-person correlation is well defined even with homogeneous personas; the item-level readout additionally survives persona homogeneity.

PART 2 -- Product judgments
You are shopping for a pair of headphones. Two models are on the shelf. You know nothing about either brand and the packaging gives no technical detail. The only thing that distinguishes them is the price.

Model K costs 189 euro.
Model T costs 39 euro.

How good do you expect the sound quality and durability of each model to be? Rate each from 1 to 9, where 1 = very poor quality and 9 = excellent quality.

PRICE_LOW: <number 1-9>

conditions.scarcity: Regional water authorities confirmed this week that reservoir levels have fallen to their lowest point in forty years. conditions.control: Regional authorities confirmed this week that the resurfacing of the ring road has been completed on schedule. ANCHOR CONVENTION: the comparison target is the FReD-recorded pair (r_o, n_o) vs (r_r, n_r). The original paper's own reported statistics (t, F, d, eta^2) are quoted only as plausibility checks on simulated levels and are NOT assumed to reconcile with r_o under a single conversion -- FReD's n_o and the paper's df sometimes refer to different studies or subsamples. Every non-reconciling case is listed in P2_log_11_21.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. RECONCILIATION: r_o = .2236 at n_o = 149 implies t ~= 2.78 on df = 147; the full text is paywalled (doi_resolve returned HTTP 403) so no printed statistic could be quoted. Treated as NOT independently verified.

The abstract supplies the claim and its direction: scarcity decreases consumers' tendency to use price to judge product quality, across multiple product categories and multiple operationalisations of scarcity. Every non-reconciling case is listed in P2_log_22_32.md, section 'FReD statistic reconciliation'. RECONCILES: Experiment 1 reports F(1,52) = 4.08, p = .049 for overall candidate rating, and Table 1 gives heavy M = 5.80 (SD 0.76, n = 26) vs light M = 5.38 (SD 0.79, n = 28) on a 1-7 scale, i.e. d = 0.54 -> r = 0.27, matching FReD's r_o = .261 (n_o = 54 = 26 + 28) to within rounding.
protocols.notes: [TRANSCRIPTION A -- written by the primary transcriber from the method section / paradigm knowledge.] Full text retrieved from PMC (PMC3005631); Experiment 1 method, F test and Table 1 cell means read directly. Between-subjects, single manipulated variable (clipboard weight), everything else identical -- Ackerman Experiment 1 design. A text-only persona has no tactile channel, so the weight must be stated in words, which converts a nonconscious haptic prime into an explicitly described sensation and introduces a demand cue that the original design specifically avoided. The protocol is retained (skip = false) because the manipulation is still deliverable as a semantic cue and the claim is testable, but any simulated effect must be read as an effect of a DESCRIBED weight, not of felt weight; this is the single largest construct deviation in rows 22-32 and is logged as such. conditions.fiction: STORY -- The bell over the door of the hardware store rang at four minutes past six, and Ada knew before she turned around that it was him. She had rehearsed this for eleven years, standing at this counter, sorting screws into their little wooden drawers, and now that the moment had arrived her hands went on sorting without her. He had lost most of his hair. He was holding a paper bag with something heavy in the bottom of it. 'I need a hinge,' he said, as though hinges were the reason a man crosses two states. Ada put down the screws. Behind him, through the glass, the light was going orange over the grain elevator, the same light as the evening he left, and she found that she was not angry, which frightened her more than anger would have. 'What kind of hinge,' she said. He set the bag on the counter and did not answer, and in the long quiet she understood that he had no idea either, that he had driven all this way with a broken thing in a bag and no name for it, and that this was as close to an apology as she was ever going to be given.
conditions.nonfiction: ARTICLE -- The hinge is among the oldest machines still in daily use. Bronze pivot fittings recovered from the eastern Mediterranean date to roughly the fourteenth century BCE, and the underlying principle -- a fixed axis about which a leaf rotates -- has not changed since. Early doors turned on a projecting stone or wooden pin seated in a socket cut into the threshold, an arrangement that carried the door's weight vertically and wore a characteristic circular groove into the stone; archaeologists use those grooves to establish which way a vanished door once swung. The butt hinge familiar today, two rectangular leaves joined by a knuckle and pin, spread through Europe with mass sheet-metal working in the eighteenth century. Its dominance is a matter of load transfer: the leaves let the door's weight be carried in shear by the frame rather than by the threshold, which is why a butt-hinged door can be made larger and thinner than a pivoted one. Modern variants -- the concealed cup hinge, the continuous piano hinge, the spring-loaded closer -- are all solutions to the same problem of keeping a moving edge aligned with a fixed one.
